claims.text: A chromium-rich passive film composed mainly of Cr2O3 forms on corrosion-resistant stainless or duplex steels.
A dense Cr2O3 passivation film provides corrosion resistance to stainless steel and Fe-Cr alloys.
The Cr2O3 film is self-healing and continuously renewed by chromium diffusing along grain boundaries.
The dynamically renewed Cr2O3 film is the primary corrosion-protection mechanism in the stated chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
Conventional stainless or duplex steels typically have a coarser grain structure than the proposed refined condition.
Controlled grain refinement increases grain-boundary density.
Increased grain-boundary density promotes rapid chromium diffusion from the steel interior to the surface.
Grain-boundary-mediated chromium transport enables continual formation and repair of the Cr2O3 passive film.
The protective Cr2O3 layer suppresses dissolution and degradation of the underlying metal.
Fine-grained steels will develop thicker and more uniform Cr2O3 layers than coarse-grained steels.
Fine-grained steels with optimized chromium content will corrode more slowly than coarse-grained or lower-chromium counterparts.
Conventional-grained steels with standard chromium levels have only moderate passive-film stability and higher corrosion rates under the same conditions.
Oxide formation is thermodynamically favored across the listed elevated-temperature, humid, chloride-containing, and molten-salt environments.
The proposed protection should operate at moderate to high temperatures when sufficient oxygen is available.
Maintaining chromium above approximately 10-12 wt% is required for the proposed mechanism.
Extreme environmental conditions that alter oxide thermodynamics can invalidate Cr2O3-based protection.
Chromium depletion and dissolution can increase substantially with temperature during molten-salt exposure.
Failure of fine-grained, high-chromium samples to show both improved Cr2O3-film behavior and lower corrosion rates relative to controls would falsify the proposed grain-boundary-diffusion mechanism.
